listen.script: I was planning to fly to Jeddah on Thursday, but now that my cousin's graduation has been moved to the following week, there's not much point going before then. Mind you, fares shoot up during the holidays, so I might just book now for the later date and stay a bit longer than I'd originally planned.
listen.q: What is the speaker most likely to do?
options: Cancel the trip because the graduation has been postponed
Book a ticket now for a later flight
Fly to Jeddah on Thursday as originally planned

listen.script: Well, the museum trip was fine, I suppose. The guide obviously knew what she was talking about, but she rushed through the Nabataean section, which, to be honest, was the part most of us had come to see. Next time, I'd rather go on my own and take my time.
listen.q: How does the speaker feel about the trip?
options: Disappointed that the most interesting part was hurried
Impressed with the trip as a whole
Annoyed that the guide lacked knowledge

read.passage: For decades, the deserts of the Arabian Peninsula were regarded as little more than empty space, places to be crossed rather than studied. That view is now changing. Researchers have discovered that sand dunes support a surprising variety of life, from beetles that collect moisture from morning fog to plants whose roots stretch several metres underground in search of water. Some scientists argue that understanding how these organisms survive could help engineers design buildings that stay cool without consuming vast amounts of electricity. Others, however, warn that rapid development, including off-road driving and large-scale tourism, threatens fragile ecosystems before they have even been properly documented. The challenge, they suggest, is not whether people should visit the desert, but how they can do so without destroying the very features that make it worth visiting.

qs.q: What does the writer suggest about the traditional view of deserts?
options: It overlooked how much life deserts actually contain
It was mainly concerned with the dangers of crossing them
It has always been shared by scientists

qs.q: According to the final sentence, what is the main issue facing the desert?
options: Whether tourism should be banned completely
Finding responsible ways for people to visit
Persuading more people to visit the desert

speak.prompt: Some people say social media has made teenagers more connected but less able to concentrate. To what extent do you agree? Give reasons and examples from your own experience or from people you know.
speak.expect: The learner can develop a clear, structured argument with relevant supporting detail and examples, weighing advantages and disadvantages (B2+). They speak fluently and spontaneously with only occasional hesitation while searching for expressions, and they use linking devices (e.g. 'on the other hand', 'having said that', 'that's not to say') to mark clear relationships between ideas. They show a good range of vocabulary for abstract topics (e.g. 'attention span', 'distraction', 'peer pressure'), with some flexibility in paraphrasing, and good grammatical control including conditionals, modals of speculation and some complex sentences. Errors are rare and do not cause misunderstanding. They can express degrees of agreement and qualify their opinion rather than giving a simple yes/no answer. Pronunciation is clear, with mostly natural stress and intonation.
